scenario.title: Two reports, one real change
scenario.intro: A maize project in western Kenya and a wheat project in South Asia both report success. The maize team can show 40 demonstration plots, 600 field-day participants and a surge in reach every quarter. The wheat team reports fewer farmers but can show which of them changed their sowing date, and what happened to their yields afterwards. Both call it a result. This module gives you the test that tells them apart.

objectives.text: Define each of the four results levels (processes, outputs, outcomes, impact) and give one example of each.
Classify a project result or indicator by results level, including policy change.
Distinguish reach from quality and explain why counting people is not measuring change.
Use an indicator crosswalk to connect project, investor and institutional indicators without silent redefinition.
Write a measurement plan row with unit, source, method, frequency, coverage, disaggregation, owner and timing.
State who owns evidence at each results level and what central MEAL adds.

lessons.title: Four levels, four kinds of evidence

beats.hook: Two projects reported success. Only one measured change. The difference is which level of the results chain each of them was describing.

example.title: One maize project across the four levels
body: Processes. The team coordinates trials with two seed companies, tracks its workplan and manages the budget. Evidence comes from workplans, financial records and the partnership registry. Owner: the project team.

Outputs. A drought-tolerant variety is released, 40 demonstration plots are established and 600 farmers attend field days. Evidence comes from delivery records, trial results and training logs. Owner: the project team, with KPI definitions and deduplication rules from central MEAL.

Outcomes. A season later, follow-up visits find that 35% of field-day participants planted the new variety and the seed companies multiply it on their own account. Evidence comes from adoption surveys and partner records. Owner: shared. The project collects, central MEAL integrates and analyses.

Impact. Five years on, panel data show sustained yield and income gains among adopters, interpreted alongside rainfall and price data. Owner: central MEAL with science and evaluation specialists. The project supplies source data and context.
Same project, four levels, four kinds of evidence, four owners. The logic is cumulative, but no level is proof of the next one.

bullets: Processes enable delivery, outputs are what is delivered, outcomes are what changes for people and systems, impact is lasting change in agrifood systems.
Each level has its own data sources and products. Different levels, different evidence.
Projects own process and output evidence. Outcomes are shared. Impact sits with central MEAL and specialists.

source.title: The MEAL Framework: From Data to Impact

lessons.title: Output or outcome? The classification test

beats.hook: "Farmers trained" feels like a result. It is. But at which level? Get this wrong and the whole results framework reports the wrong thing.

example.title: Sort eight results into their levels
example.prompt: Drop each result into the level the framework assigns it. Ask: was it done, was it delivered, did something change, or did the change last?

bins.label: Processes
bins.hint: Activities, partnerships and management actions that enable delivery.

bins.label: Outputs
bins.hint: Products, services, technologies and capacity delivered.

bins.label: Outcomes
bins.hint: Changes in behaviour, practice, systems, capacity or policy.

bins.label: Impact
bins.hint: Positive, lasting change in agrifood systems.

cards.label: Four coordination meetings held with the extension service
cards.why: Coordination is a management action that enables delivery. Nothing has been delivered yet.

cards.label: A drought-tolerant maize variety released
cards.why: The framework lists varieties developed as outputs: products delivered through projects and partnerships.

cards.label: 600 farmers attended field days
cards.why: Training delivered is an output. Attendance says nothing yet about what the farmers do next.

cards.label: 35% of participants planted the new variety the next season
cards.why: Adoption is a change in practice among beneficiaries. That is the outcome level.

cards.label: A seed company now multiplies the variety on its own account
cards.why: A partner changed its behaviour and its business system. Outcome.

cards.label: The ministry adopted the fertiliser guideline into national extension materials
cards.why: Policy implementation is explicitly listed as an outcome example.

cards.label: Household incomes among adopters remain higher five years later
cards.why: Lasting change in incomes, interpreted alongside other factors, is impact.

cards.label: Procurement of trial inputs completed on schedule
cards.why: Workplan execution and procurement are process evidence with immediate management value.

bullets: Was it done? Process. Was it delivered? Output. Did something change for people, partners or systems? Outcome. Did the change last? Impact.
Training, tools and seed are delivered. Adoption, policy implementation and new partner behaviour are changes.
Counting a delivery more often does not move it up a level.

lessons.title: Reach versus quality: counting people is not measuring change

beats.hook: A dashboard shows reach rising every quarter. The adoption survey shows no change in practice. Which one is lying? Neither. They measure different things.

example.title: Two reports of 3,000 farmers reached
body: Report A: "3,000 farmers reached through 20 training events." That is the whole record.

Report B: "3,000 farmers reached through 20 training events in three districts; 54% women; each participant registered with a persistent identifier; delivery quality scored by a post-session check; 2,100 received the full two-day module and 900 a half-day version."

Both counts are outputs. Neither is evidence of adoption. But Report B shows where, to whom, with what quality and at what scale the training was delivered. That is the foundation the framework asks for, because a season later you can link those 3,000 identifiers to an adoption survey and ask what changed, for whom.
Report A cannot be linked to anything. Its 3,000 might include the same farmer counted at three events.

bullets: Counting what was delivered is the starting point, not the result.
Output evidence should show where, how, to whom, with what quality and at what scale.
Reach rising while adoption stays flat means delivery is growing and change is not yet shown.

beats.hook: A policy brief is published. A regulation is revised. A guideline is used by every extension agent in the country. Three events, three different levels.

example.title: From policy brief to policy in use
body: A wheat project in South Asia works with a national seed regulator. Over two years it produces a policy brief on faster variety release (output: a recommendation produced), the regulator revises its release procedure using that evidence (outcome: a partner's system changed) and, two seasons later, new varieties reach farmers a year earlier than before (a further outcome: a stronger service delivery system).
Whether that leads to lasting productivity or income gains is an impact question. It needs its own evidence, interpreted alongside other factors. The revised procedure does not prove it.
The trap runs both ways. Publishing the brief is not a policy outcome. And a policy outcome, however important, is not yet impact.

bullets: Producing policy advice is an output. A partner implementing a policy is an outcome.
Policy implementation and stronger service delivery systems are explicit outcome examples in the framework.
Impact still needs evidence of lasting change in agrifood systems.

lessons.title: Crosswalks: one project indicator, several reporting frames

beats.hook: CGIAR wants one number. The investor wants a slightly different one. Your dashboard wants a third. Do you collect three times? No. You build a crosswalk.

example.title: A crosswalk for one adoption result
body: Project measure: number of registered farmers who planted the new variety on at least one plot in the 2027 main season, by gender and district.

Institutional KPI: participants adopting an improved variety, as defined in the Toolbox reference sheet (unit: farmer; method: adoption survey or verified registry; disaggregation: gender, age, territory).
Investor indicator: "farmers using improved seed", defined by the investor as any farmer who received seed from the project.
CGIAR PRMS: innovation use, reported under the relevant results framework category.

The crosswalk row records how the four relate: the project measure feeds the institutional KPI directly; the investor definition is broader (receipt rather than use) so the project reports it separately from the same registry, with the difference noted; the PRMS entry is generated from the institutional KPI by the central mapping. The institutional definition is never quietly changed to match the investor template.

bullets: The indicator crosswalk maps applicable institutional KPIs, investor indicators and project-specific measures to each other.
Projects may set local scope. They may not silently redefine an institutional indicator.
Same validated records, several reporting frames: collect data once.

beats.hook: An indicator with a name and a target is a wish. An indicator with a measurement plan row is a commitment someone can act on.

example.title: What belongs in the row?
example.prompt: The minimum package lists what a measurement plan must specify for each indicator. Sort these items into the row or out of it.

bins.label: Belongs in the measurement plan row
bins.hint: Required by section 5.4 for every indicator.

bins.label: Belongs somewhere else
bins.hint: Useful, but it lives in another document.

cards.label: Unit of observation: plot
cards.why: The unit of observation is the first field of the row.

cards.label: Data source: crop cuts on sampled plots
Valid method: net-plot harvest adjusted to standard moisture
cards.why: The method must be one the KPI reference sheet accepts.

cards.label: Disaggregation: gender of plot manager, district
Owner: Project MEAL Focal Point; timing: within four weeks of harvest
cards.why: Responsible owner and timing complete the row.

cards.label: Annual target: 4.2 t/ha
cards.why: Targets belong in the results framework, not the measurement plan row.

cards.label: Dashboard layout for the investor report
cards.why: Visualisation is designed later from the collected records.

cards.label: Budget line for enumerator days
cards.why: The cost sits in the MEAL budget, not the measurement plan.

bullets: A measurement plan row names unit of observation, source, valid method, frequency, sample or coverage, disaggregation, owner and timing.
It is part of the minimum package every project leaves inception with.
Targets, budgets and dashboards live elsewhere.

storyboards.title: Four levels, four kinds of evidence

frames.narration: Two projects reported success. Only one measured change.

scene.title: Count or change?
scene.subtitle: Two projects. Two reports. One measured change.

frames.narration: The framework sorts evidence into four levels. Processes enable delivery. Outputs are what is delivered. Outcomes are what changes for people and systems. Impact is lasting change in agrifood systems.
Watch six results find their level. Trials coordinated: a process. Variety released: an output. Farmers adopting: an outcome. Incomes sustained: impact.
Here is the one everyone gets wrong. Farmers trained tries to land in outcomes. It bounces back. Training is delivered. Adoption is a change.
Even inside outputs, there are two ways to look. Reach counts how many. Quality asks where, to whom, how well and at what scale. Only the second side gives you a foundation for outcome evidence.
Each level has its own data, its own products and its own owner. Projects own processes and outputs. Outcomes are shared. Impact sits with central MEAL and specialists.
Four questions sort any result. Was it done? Was it delivered? Did something change? Did the change last?
Apply the test. A digital advisory tool is deployed: delivered, so an output. Farmers change their planting date after using it: a change, so an outcome.
Partners count too. A seed company multiplying the variety on its own account has changed its behaviour. A ministry adopting a guideline has changed a policy. Both are outcomes.
When in doubt, ask who or what changed. If the answer is nobody yet, you are still at output level.

scene.title: Who or what changed?
scene.subtitle: If the answer is nobody yet, it is an output.

frames.narration: Reach is a count. Three thousand farmers, twenty events. The number rolls up nicely.
Quality asks what the count hides. Where were they? Who were they? How well was it delivered? At what scale? Report B answers each question and records an identifier for every participant.

scene.gap: Only B can be linked to an adoption survey

frames.narration: When reach rises and adoption stays flat, nothing is wrong with the data. Delivery is growing. Change has not been shown. Say exactly that.

scene.gap: Delivery up. Change not yet shown.

frames.narration: A policy brief is written and published. That is a recommendation produced: an output.
The regulator revises its release procedure using that evidence. A partner's system changed. Policy implementation is an outcome.

Two seasons later, varieties reach farmers a year earlier. Stronger service delivery: still an outcome. Whether yields and incomes rise and stay up is the impact question, and it needs its own evidence.
One adoption result. Four places it has to appear: the institutional KPI, the investor template, the CGIAR system and the project's own dashboard.

The crosswalk is a table that says how each one relates to the others. Where definitions differ, it records the difference instead of hiding it. The institutional definition stays as the Toolbox wrote it.
Relabelling is not harmonising. Shared definitions are. If a label is the only thing two indicators share, the crosswalk must say so.

scene.title: Same label is not same meaning
scene.subtitle: Map the definitions. Keep the institutional one intact.

frames.narration: Here is an indicator as it often arrives: a name and a target. Nobody can collect it from this.

Section 5.4 lists what the row needs. Unit of observation: plot. Source: crop cuts. Method: net-plot harvest at standard moisture. Frequency: each main season. Coverage: 240 sampled plots in three districts. Disaggregation: gender of plot manager. Owner: the Focal Point. Timing: within four weeks of harvest.
Eight fields. One row per indicator. It is part of the minimum package, so it is finished at inception, not at reporting time.

scene.title: Eight fields, one row
scene.subtitle: Finished at inception, not at reporting time.

misconceptions.description: You picked something that was delivered (training, a tool, seed, advice) when the question asked for a change in behaviour, practice, policy or systems.
You treated a management activity such as coordination, procurement or workplan tracking as a delivered product or service.
You treated a change in practice, policy or partner behaviour as proof of lasting change in agrifood systems.
You treated the number of people reached as evidence that something changed for them.
You tried to make indicators comparable by giving them the same name instead of mapping their definitions.
You accepted an indicator list without saying how, when, from whom and by whom each one is measured.

questions.question: A regional team records partner meetings, procurement steps and workplan milestones. At which results level does this evidence sit?

options.text: Outcomes
Processes
Impact
Outputs

questions.explanation: Processes are the activities, partnerships and management actions that enable delivery, including workplan implementation, coordination and financial tracking. This evidence has immediate management value but says nothing about what was delivered or what changed.
questions.reviewTip: List the process examples in section 2.1 and compare them with the output examples in 2.2.

questions.question: Which list contains only outputs as the framework defines them?

options.text: Varieties developed, digital tools deployed, training delivered, datasets published
Farmers adopting, policies implemented, incomes rising, capacity improving
Workplans executed, partners engaged, budgets tracked, risks managed
Food security improved, emissions reduced, resilience strengthened, inclusion widened

questions.explanation: Outputs are the products, services, technologies and capacity delivered through projects and partnerships. The other lists mix outcomes, processes and impact-level changes.
questions.reviewTip: Read the first sentence of section 2.2 and its list of examples.

questions.question: A seed company that partnered with the project now multiplies the new variety on its own account. Which results level is this?

options.text: Output
Process
Outcome
Impact

questions.explanation: A partner changed its behaviour and its business system, which the framework classes as an outcome. It is not yet evidence of lasting change in agrifood systems.
questions.reviewTip: Ask who or what changed. If a partner changed its behaviour, the result is an outcome.

questions.question: Five years after release, household panels show sustained income gains among adopters that persist after project closure. Which level does this evidence most directly describe?

options.text: Processes
Outputs
Outcomes
Impact

questions.explanation: Impact is positive, lasting change in agrifood systems, including incomes. Sustained gains measured over years, interpreted alongside other factors, sit at this level.
questions.reviewTip: Check the impact definition for the word lasting.

questions.question: A training log shows 1,200 participants. What does that count establish on its own?

options.text: That training was delivered, not that any practice changed
That 1,200 farmers adopted the recommended practice
That the project's outcome target has been met
That the project contributed to income gains

questions.explanation: A report can confirm that training took place or that farmers were reached. It cannot by itself show whether practices changed or benefits followed.

source.title: A New MEAL Approach for CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Separate the delivery count from the question of what changed afterwards.

questions.question: Which addition turns a bare delivery count into output evidence that can support later outcome work?

options.text: A narrative summary without participant records
Where, to whom, with what quality and at what scale it was delivered
A higher total reported more often
Relabelling the count as adoption

questions.explanation: Counting what was delivered is the starting point. Showing where, how, to whom, with what quality and at what scale is the foundation for outcome-level evidence.
questions.reviewTip: Read the last paragraph of section 2.2.

questions.question: A ministry adopts the project's recommended fertiliser guideline into national extension materials. Which results level is this?

options.text: Output, because the project produced the guideline
Process, because it involved coordination with the ministry
Impact, because national materials are lasting
Outcome, because a partner implemented a policy

questions.explanation: Policy implementation is an explicit outcome example in the framework. The guideline itself was an output; its adoption by the ministry is the change.
questions.reviewTip: Find policy implementation in the outcome examples of section 2.3.

questions.question: An investor template asks for "farmers trained" while the institutional KPI counts participants in capacity development, disaggregated by gender. What does the crosswalk do?

options.text: Replaces the institutional KPI with the investor label so that both reports show one number
Reports both numbers side by side without recording how the two definitions relate
Maps the investor indicator to the institutional KPI and project measure, keeping the institutional definition
Rewrites the institutional definition to match the investor template for this project

questions.explanation: The indicator crosswalk links applicable institutional KPIs, investor indicators and project-specific measures with no silent redefinition of institutional indicators. Differences are recorded, not hidden.
questions.reviewTip: Read the indicator crosswalk element of the minimum package.

questions.question: Which set of fields belongs in a measurement plan row?

options.text: Indicator name, target, deadline and investor contact
Budget line, staff name, dashboard and report format
Activity, output, outcome and impact statements
Unit of observation, source, valid method, frequency, coverage, disaggregation, owner and timing

questions.explanation: Section 5.4 specifies these eight fields for each indicator in the measurement plan. Targets, budgets and dashboards belong in other documents.
questions.reviewTip: Read element 3 of the minimum package.

questions.question: In the division of responsibility, who is the primary operational owner of outcome evidence?

options.text: Shared: project teams generate and collect, central MEAL integrates and analyses
Project teams alone, as for processes and outputs
Central MEAL alone, as for impact
The Data Group, which owns the data system

questions.explanation: The outcome row of the division-of-responsibility table is shared. Projects generate and collect, and central MEAL designs methods, integrates across projects and analyses.

source.title: Division of Responsibility: Project Delivery vs. Institutional MEAL

questions.reviewTip: Read the four rows of the table in section 5.2.

questions.question: Why does the framework call outcomes the level where CIMMYT's contribution is most important to establish credibly?

options.text: They are the easiest level to count from delivery logs
They are the only level that investors ask about
They show whether people, organisations and systems are changing as a result of the interventions
They remove the need for impact evidence

questions.explanation: Outcomes answer the essential institutional question: are people, organisations and systems changing as a result of CIMMYT's interventions? That is where contribution first becomes visible.
questions.reviewTip: Read the boxed question at the end of section 2.3.

questions.question: A project reports that 40 demonstration plots were established and 600 farmers attended field days. Which results level do these figures describe?

options.text: Processes
Outputs
Outcomes
Impact

questions.explanation: Demonstration plots and field-day attendance are products and services delivered, which the framework classes as outputs. They do not yet show any change in practice.
questions.reviewTip: Apply the test: was it delivered, or did something change?

questions.question: Follow-up visits find that 35% of field-day participants changed their planting date as recommended. Which results level does this evidence describe?

options.text: Impact
Processes
Outputs
Outcomes

questions.explanation: A change in agronomic practice among beneficiaries is an outcome. Whether the change leads to lasting benefit is a separate impact question.
questions.reviewTip: Compare the outcome examples in 2.3 with the impact definition in 2.4.

questions.question: The partner engagement log shows four coordination meetings and a signed memorandum with the extension service. Which results level is this?

options.text: Processes
Outcomes
Outputs
Impact

questions.explanation: Coordination and partner engagement are management actions that enable delivery, so they are process evidence. A memorandum formalising a partnership can count as an output once delivered, but meetings themselves are processes.
questions.reviewTip: Check the process examples: coordination, partner engagement, workplan execution.

questions.question: Which statement matches the framework's definition of impact?

options.text: Delivery of products, services and technologies at scale across the project area
Changes in partner behaviour, practice or policy observed during the project
Positive, lasting change in agrifood systems such as productivity, incomes or resilience
Completion of planned activities within budget and on time, confirmed by reports

questions.explanation: Impact is positive, lasting change in agrifood systems. The framework seeks credible evidence of CIMMYT's contribution to that change alongside other factors.
questions.reviewTip: Read the first sentence of section 2.4.

questions.question: Two projects each report 3,000 farmers reached. One can also show location, participant identity, delivery quality and scale. Why does the framework value the second report more?

options.text: It proves that adoption occurred
It provides the foundation needed for outcome-level evidence
It counts as impact evidence
It removes the need for outcome studies

questions.explanation: Output evidence should show where, how, to whom, with what quality and at what scale. That detail is the foundation for outcome-level evidence; it is not outcome evidence itself.
questions.reviewTip: Read the final paragraph of section 2.2.

questions.question: A dashboard shows reach rising every quarter while adoption surveys show no change in practice. What should the team conclude?

options.text: Reach growth demonstrates outcome success
The adoption survey must be wrong
The impact target has been met
Delivery is growing but there is no outcome evidence of change yet

questions.explanation: Reach is output evidence; adoption is outcome evidence. The two measure different things, so rising reach with flat adoption means delivery is growing and change has not yet been shown.
questions.reviewTip: Keep output and outcome questions separate when reading a dashboard.

questions.question: A national seed regulator revises its variety-release procedure using evidence the project provided. Which level is this, and why?

options.text: Output, because the project produced the evidence
Impact, because regulation is lasting
Outcome, because a partner's system or policy changed
Process, because it involved coordination with the regulator

questions.explanation: Policy implementation and stronger service delivery systems are outcome examples in the framework. The evidence the project produced was an output; the regulator's change is the outcome.
questions.reviewTip: Separate the output (evidence provided) from the outcome (procedure revised).

questions.question: A project must report the same adoption result to CGIAR PRMS, an investor and its own dashboard. What should the inception crosswalk show?

options.text: How the institutional KPI, investor indicator and project measure relate, with no silent redefinition
A single label used for all three systems regardless of definition
Three separate data collections, one per reporting system
Only the investor indicator, because it is contractual

questions.explanation: The crosswalk maps applicable institutional KPIs, investor indicators and project-specific measures to one another. Submissions are then generated from the same validated records, so data are collected once.
questions.reviewTip: Read the crosswalk element in 5.4 and the collect-once principle in 4.3.

questions.question: An investor defines an adopter as any farmer who received seed, while the institutional KPI counts farmers who planted it. What does the crosswalk approach allow?

options.text: Quietly adopting the investor definition for the institutional KPI
Recording the mapping and the difference, and reporting each measure under its own definition
Choosing whichever definition yields the larger number
Dropping the institutional KPI from the project

questions.explanation: Projects may specify local scope and report investor measures, but they do not silently redefine the institutional indicator. The crosswalk records the relation and the difference.

source.title: One KPI, Multiple Valid Measurement Levels

questions.reviewTip: Read the sentence in 3.2 about local scope and silent redefinition.

questions.question: A measurement plan row for "area under improved varieties" names the indicator and a target but nothing else. What is missing?

options.text: A dashboard design and a reporting template
A budget line and an investor contact
A theory of change narrative for the indicator
Unit of observation, source, method, frequency, coverage, disaggregation, owner and timing

questions.explanation: The measurement plan specifies these eight fields for each indicator. Without them nobody can collect the indicator consistently.
questions.reviewTip: Check an indicator in your own project against the eight fields.

questions.question: Which measurement plan row is complete for a plot-level yield indicator?

options.text: Unit: farmer; source: farmer recall interviews; method: not specified; frequency: once; coverage: volunteer households that responded; disaggregation: none; owner: enumerator team; timing: at endline
Indicator: yield; target: 4 t/ha; reporter: project lead; frequency: annual; format: investor template; coverage: all project districts; disaggregation: none recorded; timing: at reporting

Unit: plot; source: crop cuts; method: net-plot harvest at standard moisture; frequency: each season; coverage: 240 sampled plots in three districts; disaggregation: gender of plot manager; owner: Focal Point; timing: within four weeks of harvest
Source: satellite imagery; method: to be decided with the Data Group; owner: Data Group; disaggregation: none; frequency: as imagery becomes available; coverage: whole region; unit: pixel

questions.explanation: Only this row names unit, source, a valid method, frequency, coverage, disaggregation, owner and timing. The others leave method, coverage or disaggregation unspecified.
questions.reviewTip: Count the eight required fields in each option.

questions.question: Who holds primary responsibility for impact evidence, and what do projects provide?

options.text: Central MEAL with science and evaluation specialists; projects provide source data and context
Project teams alone; central MEAL provides a reporting template
Regional MEAL Leads alone; projects provide the final narrative
The Data Group; projects provide dashboard access

questions.explanation: The impact row of the division-of-responsibility table assigns central MEAL with science and evaluation specialists as owner, with projects supplying source data and context.

source.title: Division of Responsibility: Project Delivery vs. Institutional MEAL

questions.reviewTip: Read the impact row of the table in 5.2.

questions.question: A project lead argues that outcome analysis is entirely central MEAL's job and stops collecting outcome data. What does the division of responsibility say?

options.text: The lead is right: outcomes belong to central MEAL alone
Outcomes are shared: projects generate and collect, central MEAL integrates and analyses
Outcomes belong to the Data Group once the system is live
Outcomes are optional for projects below Large scale

questions.explanation: Outcome evidence is shared. Project teams generate and collect it; central MEAL designs methods, integrates across projects and supports analysis.

source.title: Division of Responsibility: Project Delivery vs. Institutional MEAL

questions.reviewTip: Compare the outcome row with the impact row in 5.2.

questions.question: A proposal describes its results chain as activities, outputs and impact, with no outcome level. What does the framework's results chain require?

options.text: Three levels are sufficient whenever the impact statement is well defined and costed
Outcomes can be merged into outputs for small projects with limited evidence budgets
Impact can be reported directly from outputs when delivery targets are met
Four levels, with outcomes capturing change in behaviour, systems, practice or policy

questions.explanation: The framework organises evidence across four levels: Processes, Outputs, Outcomes and Impact. Outcomes are where CIMMYT's contribution becomes visible, so they cannot be skipped.

source.title: The MEAL Framework: From Data to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Read the opening paragraph of section 2.

questions.question: A project claims improved food security from the number of nutrition training sessions held. Which two mistakes does this make?

options.text: It treats delivery as change, and it skips the outcome level between training and food security
It counts sessions instead of participants, and it omits the budget
It reports too rarely, and it uses the wrong unit of observation
It uses an institutional KPI, and it lacks a target

questions.explanation: Training sessions are outputs. Food security is an impact-level change. The claim jumps from delivery to lasting change without evidence of any outcome in between.
questions.reviewTip: Trace the claim through all four levels and find the gaps.
